lessons.title: Types, purpose and structure of teams
lessons.html:
What a team is

A team is a group of people who share a common goal, depend on each other to reach it and hold themselves jointly responsible for the result. A group of workers who simply happen to be in the same orchard is not yet a team; a picking crew that plans its rows together, shares bins and is paid on combined quality is.

Types of teams in agriculture and extension

TypePurposeExample
Work or production teamOngoing daily tasksMilking crew, pruning team, feedlot processing team
Project teamA task with a start and endBuilding a new packshed, setting up a community garden
Cross-functional teamCombining different skillsExtension officer, animal health technician and economist on a livestock project
Management teamPlanning and decisionsFarm manager with section heads
Self-managed teamTeam plans and controls its own workA farmer study group that runs its own meetings
Virtual teamWorking across distanceDistrict officers co-ordinating through a WhatsApp group and online meetings
Committee or task teamSpecific responsibilityHealth and safety committee, co-operative board

Structure

Team structure includes the size of the team, the roles in it (leader, members, specialists, recorder), who reports to whom and how decisions are made. Small teams of about five to nine people usually communicate and decide more easily. Larger teams may need sub-teams with their own leaders, such as a harvest operation split into picking, transport and packshed teams.

Team roles

Apart from formal job roles, people take on informal roles: the ideas person, the organiser, the one who checks details, the peacemaker, the one who pushes for results. A strong team has a balance of these. A good leader notices which roles are missing and either develops them or fills them.

lessons.title: Leading a team in planning and carrying out work
lessons.html:
Getting the team to work together

1. Agree the goal

Make sure everyone understands what the team must achieve, by when and to what standard. Example: prune 12 hectares of plums to the farm's standard by 31 July. Explain why it matters; people work better when they see the purpose.

2. Plan together

  • Break the goal into tasks and estimate time and resources.
  • Ask the team for ideas; experienced workers often know the best way.
  • Check equipment, PPE and safety risks, for example sharp shears and ladders.

3. Allocate roles and responsibilities

Match tasks to skills and development needs. Make each person's responsibility clear: who does what, by when, and who they report to. A simple task board or duty roster helps.

TaskResponsibleDue
Sharpen and service shearsSiphoMonday
Prune blocks 1 to 3Team A, led by Thandi15 July
Chip pruningsTractor driverWeekly

4. Lead the work

  • Hold short daily briefings: plan for the day, safety points, questions.
  • Monitor progress against the plan and quality standards.
  • Support people who struggle; coach rather than shout.
  • Remove obstacles: broken equipment, late transport, missing materials.
  • Recognise good work publicly and deal with problems privately.

Leadership styles

No single style fits every situation. In an emergency, such as a fire in the veld, a directive style is needed: clear, fast instructions. When planning a new project with experienced people, a participative style draws out ideas. With a capable, self-managed study group, a delegating style lets members lead. Good leaders adjust their style to the task and to the team's experience.

Handling conflict

Conflict is normal. Deal with it early, listen to each side, focus on the problem rather than the person and agree a way forward.

lessons.title: Factors affecting teams and reviewing team effectiveness
lessons.html:
What shapes how a team works

Team dynamics

Teams often go through stages: forming (polite, unsure), storming (conflict about roles and methods), norming (agreeing ways of working) and performing (working well together). Knowing this helps a leader stay patient during storming and guide the team towards agreed norms.

Other factors

  • Culture and language: different customs about respect, age and speaking up. Use languages everyone understands.
  • Trust and communication: teams fail when information is hidden or promises are broken.
  • Motivation and rewards: individual bonuses can undermine teamwork; team-based incentives can strengthen it.
  • Workload and resources: an overloaded team with poor tools loses morale.
  • Personal circumstances: illness, family problems, transport.

Influence of organisational structure

A strongly hierarchical organisation, with many levels and decisions made only at the top, can slow teams down and discourage initiative. A flatter structure gives teams more authority. Matrix structures, where a person reports to both a district manager and a project leader, can cause confusing priorities unless roles are clearly agreed. Policies on overtime, procurement and transport also affect what a team can do. A team leader must understand these and negotiate with management when the structure blocks the team.

Reviewing team effectiveness

Review regularly, not only when things go wrong. Lead a review meeting with the team:

  1. Did we achieve the goal on time and to standard? Look at the data: hectares done, quality checks, costs.
  2. What worked well?
  3. What did not work, and why?
  4. How well did we communicate, share work and support each other?
  5. What will we do differently next time?

Create a safe atmosphere where people can speak honestly without fear. Agree actions, assign responsibilities and follow up. Record the lessons so the next team benefits.

Key points

  • A team shares a goal, depends on each other and is jointly responsible for results.
  • Match team type and structure to the purpose of the work.
  • Agree goals, plan together and make every responsibility clear.
  • Adapt your leadership style to the situation and the team's experience.
  • Teams go through forming, storming, norming and performing.
  • Review effectiveness regularly with the team and act on the lessons.
